papers.title: Two proofs and a tight Szemer\'edi--Trotter theorem
papers.abstract: The Szemer\'edi--Trotter theorem, a fundamental theorem in incidence geometry, states that $n$ points and $m$ lines in $\mathbb{R}^2$ form at most $O(m+n+m^{2/3}n^{2/3})$ incidences. Recently, Lewko and independently Miao--Xie extended the Szemer\'edi--Trotter theorem to arbitrary fields with a correction term $O(\frac{mn}{\mathfrak{p}})$ if the field has positive characteristic $\mathfrak{p}$. In this paper, we provide some geometric intuition for the two proofs and compare them. Moreover, we show how both proofs can be improved using Hasse derivatives. As a consequence, we obtain a tight upper bound over any algebraically closed field. To be specific, when the field has positive characteristic $\mathfrak{p}$, $n\leq m$ and $\mathfrak{p}^{2(k-1)}\leq m<\mathfrak{p}^{2k}$ for some positive integer $k$, the number of incidences can be bounded by \[O\left(\mathfrak{p}^{k-1}n+m+m^{2/3}n^{2/3}+\frac{mn}{\mathfrak{p}^{k}}\right).\]

papers.title: What Forms of Student Sensemaking Predict Mathematics Learning?: Student Perspectives on Opportunity, Comfort, and Utility
papers.abstract: Instructional practices that require student sensemaking of mathematics are considered critical to learning outcomes, yet strategies for measurement of this instruction at scale have yet to be established. This study aims at validating and exploring the predictive validity of three student survey measures: students' opportunity to engage with, comfort engaging with, and utility of engaging with instructional practices targeting sensemaking in mathematics. Using an initial sample of 1,955 US middle school student responses, we conducted exploratory factor analysis to establish sensemaking construct structure, identifying two distinct factors reflecting students' active and passive participation in mathematical sensemaking. We then analyzed data from an additional 3,170 surveys collected over two years in the same context to confirm measurement properties and evaluate the measures' predictive validity. The resulting measures capture students' reported opportunities to engage in sensemaking practices (Sensemaking Opportunity), their comfort with engaging in those practices (Sensemaking Comfort), and their perceived utility of those practices when tackling new or difficult math problems (Sensemaking Utility). While Sensemaking Comfort and Sensemaking Utility both showed strong predictive validity over two years, Sensemaking Utility provided the most reliable estimates of student sensemaking. These findings offer researchers and practitioners a psychometrically sound, scalable toolkit for monitoring sensemaking in mathematics classrooms with implications for both large-scale research on instructional quality and teachers' ongoing efforts to monitor and improve their practice.

papers.title: The Markov Accessibility Topology and its Probabilistic Structure
papers.abstract: In this paper, we associate a canonical topology with the transition operator of a discrete-time Markov chain. We prove that this construction defines an Alexandroff topology, called the Markov Accessibility Topology, and subsequently establish that it coincides with the Alexandroff topology induced by the accessibility relation. This establishes a direct connection between probabilistic accessibility and order-theoretic topology, allowing several classical notions from Markov chain theory to be interpreted in topological terms. Among other results, we characterize absorbing subsets as closed sets, relate irreducibility to topological connectedness and the triviality of the topology, describe minimal open neighborhoods through accessibility and hitting probabilities, and investigate the communication quotient together with its relationship to lumpability.

papers.title: New Theorems on the Pentagon and the Pentagram
papers.abstract: We prove two pencil theorems for circumcenters in Miquel's pentagon and pentagram configuration. Each construction joins five triangle centers to five centers of circles through the Miquel points. An explicit formula expresses the finite common point as an affine combination of the ten triangle centers. Its weights are signed areas divided by squared circumradii and depend only on the side directions. Their sum also detects the parallel case. When either the vertices or the outer vertices are concyclic, the finite pencil point lies on the line joining their circle center to the Miquel circle center. We also iterate the construction when the ear centers and Miquel points lie on one circle. Radical axes give the resulting collinearities, and the common circle configuration is identified with the classical branch of Morley's five circles theorem.
